Abstract— This study aims to develop a machine learning 
model to diagnose atrial fibrillation(AF) using only medical 
information that can be obtained during routine care or medical 
examinations. We obtained the age, sex, body mass index, and 
presence of hypertension, stroke, or coronary artery disease of a 
total of 404,898 subjects, including 6,661 AF patients, from UK 
Biobank data and developed and validated an XGBoost-based 
model to diagnose AF. The developed model showed an average 
AUROC of 0.785 for diagnosing AF, with the following factors 
having the greatest impact on the results, in this order: age, sex, 
hypertension, body mass index, coronary artery disease, and 
stroke. 
 
Clinical Relevance—A model that diagnoses AF based on 
simple demographic and disease status can screen suspected AF 
early from routine healthcare without dedicated tests. 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common arrhythmia, 
affecting approximately 1.7% of the world's population, and is 
thought to be driven primarily by environmental, genetic, and 
clinical factors [1,2]. The most common way to diagnose AF 
is by analyzing the electrocardiogram (ECG) waveform. 
However, AF is characterized by the fact that it doesn't last 
long after its onset, but soon disappears, which means that 
long-term ECG monitoring is required to identify the moment 
when the arrhythmia occurs [3]. Therefore, a model for 
diagnosing AF using clinical features and disease phenotypes 
acquired during medical examinations or consultations based 
on large amounts of data has been studied recently [4]. This 
approach is highly efficient as it minimizes the additional 
effort required from the patient to diagnose AF and reduces the 
burden of ECG processing. XGBoost is frequently used for 
data processing with tabular medical data such as clinical 
information [5]. XGBoost is representative tree-based 
boosting algorithms, which is known to be robust to overfitting 
and performs well in classification and prediction through 
ensemble-based learning [6]. 
 
 
This study aims to develop a machine learning model that 
can diagnose AF using only simple information obtained from 
routine healthcare activities. In this study, we design a model 
based on XGBoost to diagnose AF using only basic 
demographic and disease information such as age, sex, and 
body mass index (BMI), and develop the model and verify its 
performance using a large dataset, UK Biobank. 
II. MATERIALS AND METHODS 
A. UK Biobank 
UK Biobank is a biomedical database for health research 
consisting of genetic and physiological information from over 
500,000 people aged 40-69 in the UK, including a range of 
demographic, disease, and genetic information [7]. This study 
used demographic and disease information from 406,615 
individuals from the UK biobank to develop a diagnostic 
model for AF. UK Biobank includes demographic information 
such as sex, age, BMI, and disease information such as 
hypertension (HTN), stroke (STK), coronary artery disease 
(CAD), and AF. From the database, 6,715 patients with AF 
and 399,900 normal controls were identified. We excluded 
1,717 subjects’ record with missing data (54 AF, 1,663 normal) 
and finally used 404,898 records (6,661 AF, 398,234 normal). 
Detail demographic and disease information is represented in 
Table I. 
B. Model Development and Validation 
In developing the XGBoost model, we set the class weight 
for the atrial AF group as 59.79 (≈ 398,237 normal / 6,661 AF), 
considering the data imbalance between the normal and AF 
groups. To minimize overfitting when training the model, 10% 
of the training data set was independently separated and used 
as a validation set, which is sampled keeping the constant ratio 
of normal to AF. The binary logistic function and cross 
entropy was used as the objective function and loss function. 
respectively. For model development and validation, we used 
10-fold cross validation to obtain the average performance 
across all folds. Model development and simulations were 
performed in python version 3.10, tensorflow version 2.10.0, 
and xgboost python package version 2.0.0.

C. Evaluation Metrics 
The performance evaluation metrics to assess the detection 
performance are area under the receiver operating 
characteristic curve (AUROC), area under precision recall 
curve (AUPRC), balanced accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, 
positive predictive value, and negative predictive value. To 
account for the impact of input variables, we calculated SHAP 
(SHapley Additive exPlanations) values, which are often used 
in explainable artificial intelligence [8]. SHAP values are one 
of the interpretable descriptors for describing the predictions 
of a machine learning model, providing information about 
which characteristics contribute to explaining a particular 
predicted outcome and how. 
III. RESULTS 
Table 2 shows the average performance in 10-fold cross 
validation, and Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 shows the ROC curve (Fig. 
1(a)) and PR curve (Fig. 1(b), and SHAP plot, respectively. 
The developed model diagnosed AF with an AUROC of 
0.785±0.009, balanced accuracy of 0.716±0.009, and 
sensitivity of 0.729±0.016. The SHAP analysis showed that 
higher age and BMI, presence of HTN, CAD, and STK, and 
being male played a major role in the diagnosis of AF. Of these, 
age was the most influential (mean of |SHAP value| = 0.22), 
followed by sex, HTN, BMI, CAD and STK. 
IV. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION 
The XGBoost model trained with the UK biobank showed 
stable performance with an AUROC of 0.785±0.009. The 
positive impact of old age and male sex on AF incidence in the 
result of SHAP analysis is consistent with previous 
epidemiologic studies [9], and further suggests that BMI and 
cardiovascular disease may be associated with AF. In this 
study, the model was developed using only simple 
demographic and disease information about atrial fibrillation, 
and did not take into account genetic, environmental, and 
ethnic factors in atrial fibrillation. It is expected that future 
studies will utilize more diverse information for learning and 
develop more precise diagnostic technologies.
